facts.text: Total cost of ownership covers all costs of a capability over its life, not just its purchase price; capital cost is one-time spending on lasting assets, operating cost is recurring spending to keep running, and one full-time equivalent (FTE) is one person's work for one full year.
facts.quote: Total cost of ownership is everything a capability costs over its life, not just the purchase price; capital cost is money spent once on things that last, operating cost is money spent every month to keep running; and a full-time equivalent (FTE) is the work of one person for one full year.

facts.text: Capital items for a simulation capability include a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) bench, workstations and perpetual licenses.
facts.quote: For a simulation capability, capital items are things like a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) bench, workstations and perpetual licenses

facts.text: Operating items for a simulation capability include cloud hours, subscriptions, maintenance contracts, storage and, above all, people.
facts.quote: operating items are cloud hours, subscriptions, maintenance contracts, storage and, above all, people.

facts.text: The booklet's labor figures are per specialist per year, equivalent to FTE, although the booklet does not use the term FTE.
facts.quote: The booklet does not use the term FTE, but its labor figures are per specialist per year, which is the same unit.

facts.text: The booklet's central cost finding is that free software does not imply low total cost of ownership for a simulation capability.
facts.quote: The booklet's central cost finding is that "free" software does not mean low total cost.

facts.text: The booklet's labor-cost anchor uses United States Bureau of Labor Statistics May 2025 median wages of about USD 135,980 for software developers, USD 104,110 for mechanical engineers and USD 161,740 for computer hardware engineers.
facts.quote: United States Bureau of Labor Statistics May 2025 median wages (about USD 135,980 for software developers, 104,110 for mechanical engineers, 161,740 for computer hardware engineers)

entities.name: United States Bureau of Labor Statistics

facts.text: Using a 31.5% benefits share, the booklet estimates employer costs at roughly USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year, excluding overhead, recruiting, contractors and licenses.
facts.quote: a 31.5% benefits share, giving employer costs of roughly USD 150,000 to 260,000 per specialist per year, before overhead, recruiting, contractors and licenses.

facts.text: Several specialist years make the simulation effort a seven-figure annual program regardless of software costs.
facts.quote: Several specialist years therefore make a seven-figure annual program whatever the software costs.

facts.text: The booklet characterizes compute as comparatively cheap, estimating approximately USD 54,000 for ten cloud graphics processors running for four months.
facts.quote: Compute, by contrast, is cheap: on the order of USD 54,000 for ten cloud graphics processors running four months.

facts.text: Team headcount for the simulation program was not found in any public source.
facts.quote: Team headcount was not found in any public source [Chapter 11].

facts.text: Chapter 13's finance reviewer warns that until the simulator is trusted, the company pays both for the simulator and for the physical tests used to validate the simulator.
facts.quote: until the simulator is trusted the company pays twice, for the simulator and for the physical tests that validate it

facts.text: Chapter 13's finance reviewer reports that recurring costs for compute, labeling, weather-chamber hire, storage, notified-body fees and dealer training were not found anywhere.
facts.quote: recurring costs for compute, labeling, weather-chamber hire, storage, notified-body fees and dealer training were not found anywhere

facts.text: Chapter 13's finance reviewer warns that the simulation business case depends on unproven reuse across machine families.
facts.quote: the business case depends on unproven reuse across machine families.

facts.text: Chapter 12 recommends that the plan specify ownership, budget and licenses for sustaining models and staff after September 2027.
facts.quote: Chapter 12 asks the plan to state what happens after September 2027: ownership, budget and licenses for sustaining the models and staff.

facts.text: Physical-test savings should be counted only after the safety team agrees that a specific physical-test category can be displaced.
facts.quote: physical-test savings be counted only after the safety team agrees that a specific physical test category can be displaced

facts.text: Simulation-program costs should be estimated bottom-up after the pilots, not before.
facts.quote: costs be estimated bottom-up after the pilots, not before [Chapter 13].
